script: Dogs got the freedom I never did—until the day the owner tried to cage them.. I walked into the dog daycare one morning, and the first thing I heard was a mom yelling, "You're not feeding him enough!" (I know, right?) The kid was crying, the pup was wagging, and I thought, "Bruh, chill." Fast‑forward to now: people expect their dogs to have the same life plan as their human. Four 30‑minute walks, a "healthy" diet, a weekend "adventure" (what even is that, like a safari?). If you don't meet the checklist, you get called an abuser. (Literally insane.) And then, the same folks who throw the "you're a monster" flag will leave their dog for weeks at a boarding house because the family is "visiting." They think a kennel is a luxury spa, but it's a noise‑bomb, a stranger's house, and a place where the dog can't find a quiet spot to nap. (I know, right?) I am better than them—like, I am literally living proof that a dog can thrive on a different schedule. My boy has a massive yard. He can jump in and out whenever he wants. He comes to work sometimes to play with other dogs. He's got more toys than a toy store. He gets high‑quality kibble, treats, and the occasional table scrap (yes, that's a thing). He chases deer, turkeys, raccoons—he's a free‑spirit. The only thing that might be a bit of a "rule" is an underground fence. I trained him on it as a puppy, and now he's a pro at it. He never gets punished for digging—positive reinforcement only. And every night, he sleeps on a couch that's way more expensive than my mattress. (I know, right?) But some people still say, "You can't get a dog unless you're going to give them the life they deserve." What does that even mean? Is anyone actually capable of that? And why does it always sound like they're talking about an apartment, a few walks, and a concrete sidewalk? I get the judgment when I let my dog dig holes in the yard or sniff the food I am eating. Either they're jealous, or they don't get that a dog is a dog. He should be allowed to do dog things. I am not here to argue, I am here to remind them that my dog lives a full, happy life—just not on a rigid schedule they can't keep. And that's all the tea for today.
